nodes.text: A finite set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is called Ramsey if, for any $k\geq 1$, there exists some $d=d(A,k)$ such that in any $k$-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^d$ there exists a monochromatic copy of $A$. Characterise the Ramsey sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

#174 : [Er75f,p.108] [ErGr79] [ErGr80] [Er83c] geometry | ramsey theory Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS73] proved that every Ramsey set is 'spherical': it lies on the surface of some sphere. Graham has conjectured that every spherical set is Ramsey. Leader, Russell, and Walters [LRW12] have alternatively conjectured that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is 'subtransitive': it can be embedded in some higher-dimensional set on which rotations act transitively. Sets known to be Ramsey include vertices of $k$-dimensional rectangles [EGMRSS73] , non-degenerate simplices [FrRo90] , trapezoids [Kr92] , and regular polygons/polyhedra [Kr91] .
